title: Arthur's name only flourished in the sixth and seventh centuries—that's the strongest evidence he existed
dek: No surviving evidence can independently prove Arthur existed, but the name ‘Arthur’, as a Roman name, flourished among British nobility only during the sixth and seventh centuries—a window no historian has yet explained.
why: The episode methodically debunks popular theories about Arthur's identity—sun god, Sarmatian cataphract, Rome's final emperor—ideal for listeners who want evidence, not legend.
who: Listeners interested in medieval history and source criticism, especially those who want to see how folklore is methodically dismantled by historians yet leaves room for doubt.
skip: The opening ~2 minutes is a brand ad—skip it.

points.h: Churchill's Arthur was simply his own reflection
points.body: Churchill wrote The Birth of Britain in summer 1938, before Munich, as war clouds gathered over Europe. His Arthur was ‘a great general’ fighting invaders to preserve civilization's flame—the projection of Churchill waiting at his desk to answer his country's call once more.

points.h: The entire legend stands on fourteen sentences
points.body: The earliest surviving mention of Arthur appears in Historia Britonum by Welsh monk Nennius around 829—just fourteen lines. Every later figure (Merlin, the sword in the stone, the Lady of the Lake, Lancelot, Guinevere, Morgan le Fay) was built on this foundation. But the text itself is maddeningly vague: his title dux bellorum could mean supreme war-leader or a king's subordinate general; even his enemies' identity goes unspecified.

points.h: Some of Arthur's twelve battles happened at a river that doesn't exist
points.body: Nennius lists seven of Arthur's twelve victories at rivers; four supposedly occurred on the same river, Dubglass, in Lincolnshire. No such river exists there. Scholars now guess the real site was Scotland or near Hadrian's Wall. In one battle, Arthur allegedly carried an icon of the Virgin Mary on his shoulder—almost certainly a mistranslation of the Welsh word for shield.

points.h: Arthur was probably constructed from Welsh poetry
points.body: Skeptics note that the battle-place names often rhyme, suggesting they were lifted from Welsh verse, which was never known for strict accuracy. More damning: in the same Historia Britonum, Arthur is just one of a long line of British heroes—Brutus, great-grandson of Aeneas, and Dolabella, Cicero's son-in-law, both explicitly fictional. Arthur's twelve battles may echo the twelve apostles.

points.h: One real volcano kept the legend alive for a thousand years
points.body: The tenth-century Annales Cambriae places Arthur's final battle, Camlann, in 537 and mentions a subsequent ‘great mortality’ in Britain and Ireland. Volcanologists and climate historians later discovered that 535 saw a massive eruption with global consequences—documented in Roman and Chinese records. Whoever wrote the Annales must have accessed sources now lost to us. This is the closest thing in the entire record to hard evidence.

points.h: The nearest contemporary eyewitness says nothing about Arthur
points.body: Gildas lived during the Battle of Badon and is our closest thing to an eyewitness—yet he never mentions Arthur. He credits the victory to Ambrosius Aurelianus, ‘a man whose parents wore purple’—a Romanized Briton who rallied his people against Saxon invasion. Many historians suspect Ambrosius is the real historical figure later grafted onto Arthur.

points.h: Arthur is a Roman name—which changes the entire theory
points.body: Linguists agree Arthur derives from the Roman name Artorius, not the Celtic root arth meaning bear. This alone kills nineteenth-century claims that Arthur was a Celtic sun or vegetation god—Celtic deities always carried Celtic names. The discovery in the 1930s inspired archaeologist Collingwood's theory: Arthur was the last Romanized British military commander, ‘the last Roman who knew how to make Rome benefit Britain.’ That idea shaped Churchill's version and prompted the 1960s excavation of Cadbury Castle, which did unearth post-Roman halls and Mediterranean luxury goods.

points.h: One scholar argues the entire legend is medieval fabrication
points.body: Historian Nicholas Higham recently concluded that Nennius invented Arthur wholesale to serve Gwynedd's politics—to prove that Britons would eventually overcome wave after wave of invaders. Yet counterevidence exists: the name Arthur appeared in Britain and Ireland's royal lines, restricted strictly to the sixth and seventh centuries; centuries before and after, no one carried it. How this window suddenly opened remains unexplained. It's why the episode leans toward agnosticism rather than flatly calling Arthur pure fiction.
